meta.title: Who really said "Concern should drive us into action and not into a depression"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Pythagoras. The line is Karen Horney's, from her 1942 book Self-Analysis, trimmed from a longer sentence about concern for world conditions.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Concern should drive us into action and not into a depression'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Pythagoras. It's psychoanalyst Karen Horney, from Self-Analysis (1942), shortened from a sentence about concern for world conditions.

answer.label: Not Pythagoras — actually Karen Horney
answer.sourceLine: From Horney’s 1942 book Self-Analysis: “We may feel genuinely concerned about world conditions, though such a concern should drive us into action and not into a depression.” The popular version drops the first half of the sentence. Nothing connects it to Pythagoras, and Wikiquote lists it among his misattributed quotes.

trail: Wikiquote’s Pythagoras page ↗ lists the line under “Misattributed” and quotes the full sentence from The Collected Works of Karen Horney (1957), p. 154.

The Internet Archive holds the 1942 W. W. Norton first edition of Self-Analysis ↗. A full-text search of its scans finds the sentence “We may feel genuinely concerned about world conditions, though such a concern should drive us into action and not into a depression.”
Quotations by Women ↗ gives the same full sentence and credits it to “Karen Horney, Self-Analysis (1942).”
A Quote Investigator search ↗ for the phrase returns no article, so no specialist investigation is being overridden here.
source.excerptNote: The popular version keeps only the second half of the sentence, “Concern should drive us into action and not into a depression,” and is sometimes trimmed further to “…into action, not into a depression.”

author.name: Karen Horney
author.heading: About the real author
author.metaLine: 1885–1952 · German-born psychoanalyst who practiced in the United States
author.bio: Karen Horney was a German psychoanalyst whose later career was in the United States. She challenged parts of Freud’s theory, tracing differences between the psychology of men and women to culture rather than biology, and she is credited with founding feminist psychology. Her books for general readers include The Neurotic Personality of Our Time (1937) and Self-Analysis (1942), the source of this line.

misattribution.heading: How it got pinned on Pythagoras
misattribution.intro: This is a 20th-century psychoanalyst’s sentence, cut down to a slogan and credited to an ancient Greek philosopher. It is not in any of Pythagoras’s sayings. No source we found shows how his name first got attached.

items.why: Wikiquote’s Pythagoras page ↗ puts the line in its “Misattributed” section and credits it to Karen Horney. It does not appear among the Pythagorean sayings on that page, such as the Symbols and the Golden Verses.

Horney wrote “We may feel genuinely concerned about world conditions, though such a concern should drive us into action and not into a depression” (Quotations by Women, citing Self-Analysis, 1942 ↗). The popular version drops the opening clause, so the context of concern about world conditions is lost.

misattribution.truthLine: The words are Karen Horney’s, from her 1942 book Self-Analysis ↗, not Pythagoras’s.

context.heading: Why the source matters
lead: In 1941 Horney left the New York Psychoanalytic Institute and founded the Association for the Advancement of Psychoanalysis (Wikipedia ↗). The next year W. W. Norton published Self-Analysis, which is the source this page traces the line to.

In the full sentence, the concern is specifically about world conditions, and Horney grants that it can be genuine before she says it should lead to action rather than depression. The trimmed version keeps the advice and drops that qualification, which is how it ended up reading like an all-purpose saying that could be credited to anyone, including Pythagoras.
context.pull: Such a concern should drive us into action and not into a depression.
